basics.name: Soren Hale
basics.label: Frontend developer
basics.headline: Frontend developer shipping interfaces that feel instant.
basics.summary: Eight years building product interfaces for fintech and developer tools. React, TypeScript, and a stubborn eye on the last hundred milliseconds.
about: I build product interfaces that feel instant and stay that way. Eight years in fintech and developer tools taught me that speed is a feature, accessibility is not optional, and the best code is the code the next person can read.

My first job was email templates and landing pages in Bergen. The build took four minutes, so I fixed it at night. That is how I found out I liked the part of the work that makes everyone else faster.

Sensor charts on the GPU at Tidewater, one console in place of forty internal tools at Ledgerline, the merchant dashboard at Kestrel Pay. Every time, the number that mattered was how long a person waited.
I join a team for six to twelve weeks, agree on the number we are moving, and ship against it every Friday. When I leave, the next developer gets a written handover and code they can read.

Built the GPU charting layer for sensor data and the accessible table view behind every chart.

projects.problem: Northwind sells outdoor gear in nine countries, and four in ten carts were abandoned on the payment step. The page waited for three services before it drew anything.
projects.solution:
- The payment form now renders from the server with the cart already in it; the card fields hydrate on their own.
- The whole flow is one state machine, so a slow network can no longer leave the button in two states at once.
- Fonts, the logo and the first product image are the only things in the critical path. Everything else waits.
projects.result:
Largest Contentful Paint on a mid-range Android went from 2.9 s to 0.8 s. Completed checkouts rose 11% in the first full month, and support tickets that mention the word **stuck** fell by two thirds.

> We had been tuning the backend for a year. Soren found the two seconds in the browser in his first week.

writing.title: The last hundred milliseconds
writing.summary: Getting a page from fast to instant is a different job from getting it from slow to fast.
writing.body:
Most performance work is removal. You find the two megabyte bundle, the blocking font, the image nobody sized, and you take them away. That gets a page from four seconds to one, and it is satisfying work because every change shows up on the chart.

The last hundred milliseconds are not like that. Nothing is obviously wrong any more. The page is already fast by any score you care to run, and it still does not feel instant.

## Measure the wait, not the load

People do not experience your load event. They experience the gap between wanting something and seeing it. So I measure three moments: the first thing they can read, the first thing they can tap, and how long that first tap takes to answer.

```ts
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (entry.duration > 100) report(entry.name, entry.duration)
  }
}).observe({ type: "event", buffered: true, durationThreshold: 40 })
```

Forty lines of this in production told me more than a month of lab runs. The slow interaction was never the one I would have guessed.

## Spend the budget on purpose

- Put the answer in the first response, even if it is a cached one.
- Hydrate the thing under the thumb first.
- Let everything else arrive late and quietly.

On the Northwind checkout the pay button was the last thing to become interactive, because it sat at the bottom of the component tree. Moving it to the front of the queue cost one afternoon and was worth more than the previous two weeks.

## Know when to stop

> Fast is a number. Instant is a feeling, and it starts at about a hundred milliseconds.

Below that line people stop noticing, so I stop too. The work is boring and specific, which is why it is rarely done, and why it is worth a lot to the few products that do it.

writing.title: What a design system is actually for
writing.summary: It is not for consistency. It is for making the right thing the easy thing.
writing.body:
Every design system pitch starts with a slide of fourteen slightly different buttons. Consistency is the symptom people can see, so it is the one that gets funded.

The real job is quieter. A developer on a deadline should reach for the accessible, tested, on-brand component because it is the fastest option they have. If the system is slower than writing a div, the div wins, and no amount of governance changes that.

## Three tests I use

- Can a new developer build a settings page on day two without asking anyone?
- When the brand colour changes, is it one pull request?
- Does the system say no clearly, with a reason?

If the answer to all three is yes, the fourteen buttons take care of themselves.

## Make the right thing the short thing

Most of the work is in the types. A component that cannot be given a wrong combination of props needs no documentation for that combination.

```tsx
type ButtonProps =
  | { kind: "solid"; icon?: "arrow" }
  | { kind: "ghost"; icon?: "arrow" | "down" }
  | { kind: "quiet"; icon?: never }

export function Button(props: ButtonProps & { label: string }) {
  // three looks, and no fourth one to argue about
}
```

At Halden the token file is the single source. Colour, type and spacing are generated for the web, for the apps and for the design library from that one file. Nobody copies a hex value, so nobody copies the wrong one.

## Adoption is the product

I spend as much time with the teams as on the components: the first two screens are migrated together, and there is a weekly hour where anyone can bring a case the system does not cover. Half of those cases become a component. The other half become a written no.

A system is finished when people stop mentioning it. That took about nine months.

writing.title: An INP budget you can keep
writing.summary: How I set an interaction budget with a team, and what we do on the day it breaks.
writing.body:
Interaction to Next Paint is the first web vital that measures what a product feels like after it has loaded. It is also the easiest one to lose slowly: every feature adds a few milliseconds and no single pull request looks guilty.

## Pick the number together

I ask the team to use the product on a four year old phone for ten minutes. The number we agree on after that is always lower than the one I would have proposed. For most products it lands at 200 ms at the 75th percentile, and 100 ms for the two or three interactions that make money.

## Report the interaction, not the score

A number on a dashboard tells you that something is slow. It does not tell you what. So the report carries the element.

```ts
import { onINP } from "web-vitals/attribution"

onINP(({ value, attribution }) => {
  if (value <= 200) return
  report({
    ms: Math.round(value),
    target: attribution.interactionTarget,
    phase: attribution.inputDelay > attribution.processingDuration ? "input delay" : "handler",
  })
})
```

After a week the list sorts itself. On the Kestrel dashboard nine tenths of the slow interactions were one filter on one table.

## Make it somebody's Tuesday

A budget with no owner is a wish. Ours has a name on it each sprint and a chart on the wall. The owner does not fix everything; they notice first and ask the right team.

## When it breaks

We do not revert. We find the interaction, fix that one, and write down what caused it in a file called `slow.md` that now has thirty one entries.

- Twelve were work done on every keystroke that could wait for a pause.
- Nine were lists that rendered rows nobody could see.
- Six were third party scripts.

The file is the most useful onboarding document we have. New developers read it and stop making the first twelve mistakes.

writing.title: Code review is writing
writing.summary: The comment you leave is read by a person on a deadline. Write it for them.
writing.body:
I have reviewed a few thousand pull requests. The ones that went well had very little to do with how right I was, and a lot to do with how the comment read to a person who was tired, on a deadline and proud of the work.

## Say what you understood first

Half of all review arguments are two people describing different code. One sentence at the top removes most of them: this moves the price calculation to the server and keeps the old path behind a flag. If that sentence is wrong, the author learns something important before I have criticised anything.

## Separate must from would

I mark every comment. It takes five characters and it changes the whole conversation.

```
must:   this drops the aria-label, so the icon button has no name
should: the retry lives in three places now, worth one helper
nit:    name could say what it returns
ask:    why a ref here and not state? I may be missing something
```

A review with one `must` and six `nit` lines is an approval with homework. A review with seven unmarked comments reads as seven objections.

## Approve more than you block

- If the change is safe and better than what was there, I approve and leave the comments.
- If I would have done it differently but it works, I say so once and approve.
- I block for correctness, accessibility and anything that is expensive to undo.

## Review the description too

The pull request text is the only documentation most changes ever get. I ask for three things in it: what changed, how to see it, and what was deliberately left out. When the description is good I can review the idea first and the code second, which is the right order.

A review is a small piece of writing with one reader. Treat it like one and most of the friction goes away. The juniors on my last team started copying the prefixes within a month, and review time fell by about a third.

writing.title: Estimates that hold
writing.summary: Why I quote in ranges, what goes in the gap, and how often I have been wrong.
writing.body:
I have kept a spreadsheet of every estimate I have given since 2019, next to what the work really took. Sixty three rows. On average I was 22% under. I have not been under since I changed three things.

## Ranges, not numbers

Four to six weeks tells a client what I know and what I do not. Five weeks only pretends. The width of the range is information: a narrow one means I have built this before, a wide one means we should spend two days finding out before anyone signs.

## Name the unknowns

Every quote lists the two or three things that could move it. If one of them happens, nobody is surprised, and the conversation is about the thing rather than about me.

```
Checkout rebuild        4 to 6 weeks

Moves the range:
  - the payment provider's sandbox is as slow as last time   +1 week
  - address lookup needs a second supplier for two countries +3 days
  - design for the error states arrives after week 2         +1 week
```

Clients read that block more carefully than anything else I send.

## Ship in week one

Something real, deployed, however small. It is the cheapest way to find out what the estimate missed: the build takes nine minutes, the staging data is two years old, the login needs a ticket to another team.

## What the spreadsheet says now

- Work I had done before: within 10% every time.
- Work with one unknown: the top of the range, almost always.
- Work with three unknowns: I should have sold a discovery week instead.

The last line is the one that changed my business. A paid week of finding out is easier to sell than it sounds, and it has never once made the real quote larger than the guess would have been wrong.

repos.name: use-latency
repos.summary: A React hook that measures how long every interaction really takes, in production.
repos.body:
use-latency is a 900 byte React hook around the Event Timing API. It tells you which interactions were slow for a real visitor, and which component was under their finger at the time.

## Usage

```tsx
import { useLatency } from "use-latency"

export function App() {
  useLatency({
    over: 200,
    report: (entry) => send("/vitals", entry),
  })
  return <Routes />
}
```

## What you get

- `entry.duration` in milliseconds, measured from input to the next paint
- `entry.target` as a short selector, and the nearest component name in development
- `entry.kind`: pointer, keyboard or drag

## Why it exists

It started as a debugging script on a payments dashboard. Lab tools said the table was fine; the people using it said it was not. The hook proved them right in an afternoon.

> No dependencies. It does nothing at all in browsers without the Event Timing API.

repos.name: glyphfield
repos.summary: Draws any picture as source code on a canvas. It runs the portrait at the top of this site.
repos.body:
glyphfield draws any picture as text on a canvas. It samples the light of the image per cell and sets one glyph from the text you give it, brighter cells first. The portrait at the top of this site runs on it.

## Usage

```ts
import { glyphfield } from "glyphfield"

const field = glyphfield(canvas, {
  image: "/portrait.webp",
  text: source,       // any string, it repeats
  cell: 9,            // px
  ink: "#F1F2EC",
})

field.reveal()        // glyphs settle once
```

## Notes

- One canvas, no dependencies, 2.4 kB
- Pauses when it is off screen or the tab is hidden
- Respects reduced motion: it draws the final frame and stops

The image must be served from the same origin, or with CORS headers, because the pixels are read.

repos.name: tinyflip
repos.summary: Layout animations in 1.1 kB, using the FLIP technique and nothing else.
repos.body:
tinyflip animates layout changes with the FLIP technique: measure, change the DOM, then animate the difference with a transform. It is 1.1 kB and does not know about any framework.

## Usage

```ts
import { flip } from "tinyflip"

const play = flip(list.children)   // first: measure
list.append(list.firstElementChild) // change the DOM any way you like
play({ duration: 320 })             // invert and play
```

## Good to know

- Only `transform` and `opacity` are animated, so nothing triggers layout while it runs
- Elements that entered or left get a fade; pass `enter` and `exit` to change it
- With reduced motion the change is instant

It works with any renderer because the two calls sit on either side of whatever updates your DOM.

repos.name: a11y-probe
repos.summary: A command line check that tabs through your page and tells you where focus got lost.
repos.body:
a11y-probe opens your page in a headless browser, presses Tab until focus is back where it started and prints every stop: what was focused, whether you could see it, and the name a screen reader would announce.

## Usage

```bash
npx a11y-probe https://your-site.com/checkout --width 390

 1  a      "Skip to content"        ring ok
 2  a      "Northwind home"         ring ok
 3  button ""                       NO NAME
 4  input  "Card number"            ring ok
 5  div    (focus lost)             NOT VISIBLE
```

## What it catches

- Controls with no accessible name
- Focus that lands on something invisible or off screen
- Focus traps, and menus you cannot leave with Escape

It exits with code 1 when anything fails, so it can sit in CI next to your tests.

faq.question: When are you available?
faq.answer: I take on one main project at a time and usually book four to six weeks ahead. The status line at the top of the site is kept up to date.

faq.question: Do you work alone or with a team?
faq.answer: Both. I am often the only frontend developer on a small product, and just as often I join an existing team for a few months. For design and backend I work with people I have shipped with before.

faq.question: How do you price a project?
faq.answer: A fixed range for a defined scope, or a monthly rate for an embed. Every quote lists what is included and the two or three things that could change it.

faq.question: Do you only work in React?
faq.answer: React and TypeScript are where I am fastest. I have shipped with Svelte, Vue and plain web components, and I will tell you early if your stack is one I should not be learning on your budget.

faq.question: Can you work without a finished design?
faq.answer: Yes. I can build from wireframes and a brand guide, and I make the detailed decisions in the browser where they can be tested. For a full visual identity I bring in a designer.

faq.question: Will you work in our existing codebase?
faq.answer: That is most of my work. I start with a short audit so we both know what is there, then follow your conventions unless there is a measured reason to change one.

faq.question: What happens when the project ends?
faq.answer: You get the code, the tests, written documentation and a recorded walkthrough. I stay available for questions for thirty days at no charge.

faq.question: Which hours do you work?
faq.answer: Central European time, with a fixed overlap until 18:00 for teams in the Americas. I reply to messages within one working day.

story.title: I started with the build script nobody wanted.
Then three product teams, each one closer to the user.
Now I work on my own, one project at a time.

principleNotes: No rewrite starts before there is a number for how slow it is today. Otherwise nobody can tell when it is done.
A real deploy every week, however small. A demo that runs on my laptop is not progress.
Accessibility is part of the first build. Added at the end, it costs three times as much and still feels bolted on.
The fastest code is the code that never reaches the phone. HTML and CSS get the first try.
Decisions go in the repository, next to the code they explain. Chat threads are where reasons go to disappear.
If a deadline or a tool is wrong for the job, you hear it in week one, with the reason.

now.line: Building transactions v3 for Kestrel Pay, and booking one new project from November.

process.get: A written quote within two working days
The note, a timeline and a price range
A link you can open on your phone
A Friday build and a short written update
The docs, the recording and thirty days of questions

steps.summary: Two pages: routes, data flow, state, what gets tested and what does not. You sign it off before any code exists.
A real screen on a real URL behind a login, with CI, a preview per pull request and the performance budget switched on.
Each flow is finished before the next one starts: components, empty and error states, tests. A written update every Friday.
Docs in the repository, a recorded walkthrough and a call with whoever maintains it next.

faqs.question: Do you need finished designs?
faqs.answer: No. Wireframes and a brand guide are enough. I settle the details in the browser, where they can be tested on a real phone.

faqs.question: Who owns the code?
faqs.answer: You do, from the first commit. It lives in your repository and runs in your CI.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes?
faqs.answer: The quote lists the two or three things that could move it. If one of them happens I tell you the same day, with the new range.

steps.summary: I read what your real visitors get: the 75th percentile for LCP, INP and CLS, split by page type and device.
The slowest five journeys, traced on a mid-range Android and a three year old laptop. Every finding gets a cause, not a guess.
One list, ordered by what each fix is worth: the change, the expected gain in milliseconds and the effort in days.
The top three land as pull requests, with before and after traces, plus a budget file your CI can enforce.

faqs.question: Do you need production access?
faqs.answer: Read access to the repository and to your analytics is enough. I never need customer data.

faqs.question: What if nothing is slow?
faqs.answer: Then the report is short and says so, with the numbers. It has happened twice.

faqs.question: Can you fix everything you find?
faqs.answer: The first three fixes are included. The rest can be a follow-up build, or your team takes the list.

steps.summary: Every button, input and table that exists today, counted and grouped. The teams see their own drift on one page.
Colour, type and spacing in one file, generated for code and for the design library from the same source.
Built in the order your teams need them, each with keyboard behaviour, a usage note and visual tests.
Two real screens migrated with each team, a contribution guide and a weekly office hour that outlives me.

faqs.question: We already have a component library.
faqs.answer: Good. I start from it. Most systems need fewer components and better ones, not a rewrite.

faqs.question: Does it work with our design tool?
faqs.answer: Tokens export to the common variable formats, so the library and the code stay in step.

faqs.question: How do you get teams to use it?
faqs.answer: By making it the fastest option they have, and by sitting with them for the first two screens.

steps.summary: I ship one small fix on day two and spend the rest of the week reading the code, the backlog and the last three incidents.
I take the piece nobody has had time for: the rewrite, the migration, the slow table.
Reviews answered within a working day, two pairing slots your developers can book.
A written state of the frontend: what is solid, what is fragile and what I would do next.

faqs.question: Which days do you work?
faqs.answer: Three fixed days a week, agreed up front, with an overlap until 18:00 Oslo time for teams in the Americas.

faqs.question: Can we extend?
faqs.answer: Month by month after the first three, with thirty days notice on either side.

faqs.question: Do you join our stand-ups?
faqs.answer: Yes, on my days. On the others I read the channel and answer what is blocking.
